UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                 )
    Midcontinent Independent System              )        Docket No. ER27-25-000
    Operator, Inc.                               )


                    SUPPORTING COMMENTS OF
      THE ENTERGY OPERATING COMPANIES AND CLECO POWER LLC

        Pursuant to Rule 212 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure1, and

the Commission’s October 2, 2026, notice in the above-captioned docket, Entergy

Services, LLC, on behalf of the Entergy Operating Companies (“Entergy”)2 and Cleco

Power, LLC hereby submit comments in support of the Midcontinent Independent

System Operator, Inc.’s (“MISO’s”) filing to establish the Large Load Addition Resource

Study (LARS).

        Entergy and Cleco Power LLC support MISO’s October 2, 2026, filing to

establish the LARS process, and respectfully urges the Commission to accept it, as it will

enable MISO to expeditiously review the interconnection needs of large loads over 200

MW that have identified new generation resources to support their needs. As a general

principle, the LARS process should reduce overall interconnection-related costs to

consumers.

        Large loads, including computational data centers, advanced manufacturing, and

other energy-intensive industries, are arriving in MISO’s footprint at an increasing pace,




1
 18 C.F.R. § 385.212.
2
 The Entergy Operating Companies are Entergy Arkansas, LLC (“Entergy Arkansas”), Entergy Louisiana,
LLC (“Entergy Louisiana”), Entergy Mississippi, LLC (“Entergy Mississippi”), Entergy New Orleans,
LLC (“Entergy New Orleans”), and Entergy Texas, Inc. (“Entergy Texas”).


                                                                                                      1
 and their addition to the bulk electric system can create unique study needs. Pairing these

loads with generation that is developed to support them can be one way to reduce the

need for significant transmission upgrades that might be otherwise needed if only the

generation or only the load were interconnecting; however, to date, MISO has not always

studied such generation-load pairs in a manner that recognizes these synergies. LARS

offers a coordinated, 120-day parallel study of eligible large loads and their paired

generation resources. It is a measured and thoughtful response to the Commission’s call

for tariff provisions concerning electrically proximate large loads and generation, and it

should be accepted as just and reasonable.3

    I.      Background

         Both Entergy and Cleco Power LLC are load-serving entities with an obligation to

serve the electricity needs of their customers. The Entergy Operating Companies are

generation and transmission-owning members of MISO and serve approximately 3.1

million retail customers, 70% of which are large industrial or commercial businesses. As

load serving entities, the Entergy Operating Companies procure both generation and

transmission service for their retail customers, including large loads. The Entergy

Operating Companies own or lease over 24,000 MW of generation assets producing

electricity that is carried across more than 16,000 miles of high voltage transmission

lines.

         Cleco Power LLC is an electric utility engaged principally in the generation,

transmission, distribution, and sale of electricity within Louisiana. Cleco Power LLC is a



3
 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, (issued June 18, 2026) (Docket
No. EL26-70-000) (“Show Cause Order”); Prepared Direct Testimony of Christina Drake (“Drake
Testimony”) at 7, 41.


                                                                                                     2
 Louisiana limited liability company and a wholly owned subsidiary of Cleco Corporate

Holdings LLC, a privately held holding company. Cleco Power currently owns eight (8)

generating units with a capacity of over 2,600 MW and maintains approximately 1,380

miles of transmission lines. When the Entergy Operating Companies and Cleco Power

identify needs for new generation resources to support load growth, the decision about

where to construct the new generator is based in part on where new loads are likely to be

located. This is done to try to reduce the need for additional transmission upgrades if

possible.

           For the Entergy Operating Companies and Cleco Power, the inclusion of LARS as

an option to plan for the future needs of its growing customer base is vital. In recent

years, both companies have seen first-hand why a coordinated, expedited study pathway

is needed for new large loads that are paired with generation. MISO’s DPP cycles have

taken four years or longer to reach completion, leaving load-serving entities without a

timely path to interconnect associated generation that is being built to benefit customers

that are hoping to be served within a much shorter timeframe. That timing mismatch,

between the pace of large-load arrivals and when an associated generator can obtain a

signed GIA, is what LARS helps to resolve by aligning the load and generation on

parallel studies and on a single 120-day track.4 And, the ability to identify combined

transmission solutions and avoid the introduction of duplicative and expensive upgrades

will certainly result in far faster and clearer interconnection timelines.




4
    Id.; see also MISO Transmittal Letter at 19.


                                                                                             3
     II.      The LARS Process is Just and Reasonable

          LARS should be accepted by the Commission because it is just and reasonable

and delivers coordinated speed to power without sacrificing study integrity. By studying

load and its paired generation together, MISO can identify combined transmission

solutions, avoid duplicative and costly upgrades, and produce a reliable outcome in

approximately 120 days. This is not currently achievable across the separate EPR, DPP,

and ERAS processes and timelines that are now in place.5 Making LARS a permanent

process is appropriate because it provides needed, long-term regulatory and financial

certainty required to site and finance large load-and-generation pairings, and it includes

structural limits that keep the process bounded in every cycle.6 As further highlighted in

MISO’s filing, LARS aligns with and is directly responsive to the Commission’s Show

Cause Order, as it offers an explicit pathway for MISO to “account for the operational

dynamics of serving electrically proximate large loads.”7

          The Commission should evaluate LARS under the “independent entity variation

standard” to determine whether MISO’s variation here is just and reasonable, not unduly

discriminatory or preferential and accomplishes the purposes of Order No. 2003.8 First,

the LARS project requirements are appropriately tailored with reasonable limitations to

prevent unintended uses. LARS limits the total number of projects to ensure that MISO

  Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,064 at 2 (July 21, 2025) (Docket No.

proposed deviations from the Commission’s pro forma LGIP and pro forma LGIA are just and reasonable
and not unduly discriminatory or preferential and accomplish the purposes of Order No. 2003.”).


                                                                                                            4
 can administratively support the new process, as only ten generation/load pairs per study

period will be evaluated, with three periods per year.9 Second, MISO’s proposed tariff

revisions propose stringent eligibility requirements to deter speculative interconnection

requests and minimize disruption to the DPP, including a 150% generation to Associated

Load ceiling, a $250,000 deposit, a three-year commercial operation date, and a same-

Local-Resource-Zone requirement.10 Third, MISO’s proposal is consistent with the

Commission’s open-access goals because it is transparent, competitive, technology and

fuel agnostic, applies identical eligibility to all applicants, and does not restrict DPP

access or adversely affect DPP applicants.11 These tailored limitations demonstrate that

LARS is a reasoned approach that anticipates and resolves issues consistent with

previously stated Commission guideposts.

            In short, the Entergy Operating Companies and Cleco Power support LARS

because it is a tailored pathway that reasonably optimizes the nature of coordinated load

and generation studies, which in turn facilitates more efficient and cost-effective

transmission system planning. It is a significant step to ensure that MISO and its

stakeholders thoughtfully build the grid to meet its new large load demands. It is a

necessary new product for a new commercial reality.

     III.      Conclusion

            LARS is a timely, well-designed, and appropriately limited tool for integrating

large loads and the generation built to serve them, and it responds directly to the

 Commission’s Show Cause Order in this regard. Therefore, the Entergy Operating

Companies and Cleco Power respectfully request that the Commission accept MISO’s

LARS filing.
